item.title: The Indian state has made Bengali Muslims outsiders in their own land
item.description: Documents are meaningless with ethno-linguistic identity reason enough for arbitrary detention and even deportation of marginal workers across India.
item.content:encoded:
Reading news reports in recent weeks has made one thing clear: being a Bengali-speaking Muslim has, by itself, become incriminating in today’s India.

Simply having this ethno-linguistic identity is enough to trigger the suspicion of state officials. Amid the fervid political rhetoric about “ghuspetiya” – infiltrators – and supposed demographic change, being a Bengali-speaking Muslim has come to be associated with being an outsider.

Across the country, Bengali-speaking Muslim marginal workers are being picked up for questioning, detained and even deported to Bangladesh. For instance, last month in Bengaluru, 3,000-odd Bengali Muslim garbage and waste workers were picked up by the police as part of a massive verification drive against allegedly unauthorised migrants.

Only 31 of them were eventually determined to be Bangladeshi nationals and sent to West Bengal to be deported to Bangladesh. In Chhattisgarh, 23 workers from West Bengal – only one Hindu and the rest Muslims – were detained on suspicion of being Bangladeshi nationals this month.

In July, a Muslim woman tracing her roots to North 24 Parganas district of West Bengal was detained and deported to Bangladesh in July.

These three episodes are a continuation of a phenomenon that began last summer, when the authorities detained thousands of Bengali Muslim workers across the country, deporting hundreds to Bangladesh – mostly without trial...

item.title: Scroll’s Rokibuz Zaman wins 2026 Biswajit Roy Memorial Award
item.description: He received the prize for his reportage from the North East and West Bengal on citizenship, identity, displacement and the revision of voter rolls.
item.content:encoded:
Scroll’s Rokibuz Zaman on Tuesday won the 2026 Biswajit Roy Memorial Award for people-centric journalism.

He was awarded in the emerging journalist category for his commitment to people-centred journalism.

Zaman won the prize for his ground reporting from West Bengal, Assam and the rest of the North East on matters of citizenship, identity, displacement and the special intensive revision of electoral rolls.

His reportage has “consistently tried to put the people affected by these processes at the centre of the story, rather than treating citizenship and electoral issues only as political or statistical questions”, the organisers said.

Zaman’s reports on the citizenship crisis in Assam, “including the experiences of persons facing foreigners tribunals and citizenship scrutiny, has documented the human consequences behind what are often reduced to political or statistical debates”, they added.

item.title: J&K: Four CISF personnel shot dead by colleague in Kathua
item.description: A head constable at a power project reportedly opened fire after an argument with others in his contingent.
item.content:encoded:
Four Central Industrial Security Force personnel were killed in Jammu and Kashmir’s Kathua after their colleague allegedly opened fire at them with his service rifle following an argument, reported The Hindu.

All the personnel were posted at the Sewa Hydel-II power project. The accused head constable, Avdesh Kumar Singh, has been arrested.

It is unclear what led to the incident.

Singh and his wife work for the Central Industrial Security Force, reported The Indian Express. A police officer investigating the matter told the newspaper that Singh had an argument with his colleagues and company commander Ankit Kumar Pandey for bringing his child to the project site frequently.

“The couple worked in different shifts at the same site,” the unidentified officer added. “So, when one parent reported for duty, they would bring the toddler along to hand him over to the spouse returning home.”

The officer said that the couple was asked not to bring the child to the project site. On Tuesday, when the child was at the site, “someone complained about it to the company commander”, which led to the argument, he added.

Apart from Pandey, the others who were killed are sub-inspector Lakshman Singh and constables Sanjeev Kumar and Muhammad Rafiq.

item.title: Why India does not have enough caregivers for people with disabilities
item.description: A government scheme launched in 2015 to train caregivers was shut down in four years, with few results to show for it.
item.content:encoded:
In March 2022, Rahul Kumar’s family hired a nurse from a private agency to assist him for three days.

Kumar had been diagnosed with a motor neurone disease five years earlier. He was in his late thirties, and had begun losing sensation in his toes. Before long, he found it difficult to lift or move his feet.

While doctors did not immediately understand the cause of these symptoms, a series of diagnostic tests helped rule out possibilities such as inflammation from allergies and heavy metal toxicity. Neurological examinations eventually pinpointed his ailment.

Doctors told Kumar that the disease would cause muscles that control activities like walking, speaking, swallowing and breathing to weaken over months or years. Its progression could not be predicted, and it could not be cured. All he could hope to do through treatment was manage the symptoms.

Within five years, Kumar had become wheelchair-bound and dependent on caregivers to support his daily needs. His family hired a full-time helper who could assist him with everyday activities, as well as typing on a computer and phone. item.title: Days to go for polling, Brazil sees a lackluster election campaign
item.description: President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is running against Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of incarcerated former President Jair Bolsonaro.
item.content:encoded:
With less than two weeks to go before voters head to the polls on Oct. 4, 2026, Brazil is experiencing a presidential election campaign that is much less heated than many would expect given the high-level of polarisation in the country.

The latest polling also suggest few shifts in the political landscape, dominated by incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and his main right-wing challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of incarcerated former President Jair Bolsonaro.

But making predictions about Brazil’s presidential vote is a tricky business. In Brazil, voting is mandatory for literate citizens between 18 and 70 years of age, and if one presidential candidate doesn’t get to 50%+1 of the valid votes (not counting absentees and blank or invalid votes) in the first round, the field is narrowed to two candidates, who then face a run-off, scheduled for October 25, 2026.

The run-off is a very likely scenario in the current situation. But as a political scientist who has studied Brazilian elections for decades, I don’t think it’s safe at the moment to base analyses on existing second-round simulations, since about 30% of voters are still undecided in the first round, if spontaneous polls are to be trusted. item.title: In Pakistan, attack on mosque and its fallout reveals evolving landscape of extremist outfits
item.description: The incident has reopened the cycle of Pakistani cross-border action and Afghan retaliation.
item.content:encoded:
The suicide bombing and gun attack that killed dozens in northwest Pakistan on September 18, 2026, highlighted the fragile security situation in the South Asian country. But it also shone a light on the complex and evolving extremism landscape there and the strained relationship between Pakistan and neighboring Afghanistan.

The assault took place as worshipers gathered for Friday prayers in the city of Kohat, in Khyber Puktunkhwa province, northwest Pakistan. A suicide bomber rammed an explosives-laden car through the wall of a police complex in the city of Kohat, targeting the mosque inside. Gunmen then exchanged fire with law enforcement officials during a 20-hour standoff. In all, 31 people were killed, including 16 police officers, while over 100 people were reported injured.

Supporters of the militant group Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan, or IMP, claimed responsibility on encrypted apps like Telegram. But other seemingly aligned groups distanced themselves from the attack. Pakistan responded by conducting airstrikes in Afghanistan, home to at least one of the gunmen.

Over the past two years, we have conducted fieldwork in this region and closely monitored the operational and propaganda activity of violent extremist groups, including the Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan. The attack and its fallout reveal much about the state of collaboration and friction among the various militant entities that have fueled violence.

“Preliminary questioning indicates that they were in contact with certain associations for facilitating their registration and renewal in lieu of illegal gratification,” the ministry added.

item.description: The slur ‘pajeet’ and its variants appeared in 30% of all posts on social media platform X and 45% of mentions on fringe websites.

Online hate in the United States against South Asians surged 240% between January 2024 and June 2026, according to a study by Washington-based think tank Center for the Study of Organized Hate.

More than half a million posts with racist, dehumanising and xenophobic slurs and narratives targeting South Asians appeared on social media platform X between January 2025 and June 2026, found the study published on Monday.

The monthly volume had risen by 75% during this period and 240% between January 2024 and June 2026, it added.

Such posts had “dramatically increased” across mainstream and fringe social media platforms, the study found.

The study examines the scale, nature and tactics of online hate targeting South Asian Americans, including those of Indian, Pakistani, Bangladeshi and other South Asian backgrounds across social media platforms such as X, 4chan, 8chan and Gab.

The think tank identified nearly four lakh hateful and dehumanising posts targeting South Asians across platforms such as 4chan, 8chan and Gab in 2025.

The beverage maker’s Indian subsidiary argued before the High Court that the “abrupt prohibition” was affecting its existing and planned investments in India. It also alleged that the regulator had not followed due process before reaching its decision.

item.title: Harsh Mander: How cow slaughter bans have annihilated farm, meat and leather livelihoods
item.description: Outlawing beef is driven by religious and political motivations but hits poor and marginalised groups the hardest.
item.content:encoded:
The gentle cow – beloved in the Indian tradition for millenia – has today been weaponised by Bharatiya Janata Party governments and Hindutva mobs. Weaponised for hate and fear, for lynching, for incarceration, for erasure and for mass impoverishment.

Cow slaughter is now legal only in eight states, including Kerala, Goa, West Bengal, Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Nagaland, Mizoram and Tripura. Most other states under Bharatiya Janata Party governments have seen cow protection laws from the past made harsher, more stringent, and punishments comparable or higher than those for manslaughter.

In many states, the definition of the cow has been widened to include more bovines including those that become unproductive, trade and often even the transport of cows been criminalised, the role of “vigilante” groups in working with the police to enforce the ways legitimised, the powers of the police massively broadened, and punishments for violations rendered much more severe.

item.title: Beyond the myth of India’s Sanskrit-speaking villages, can the language anchor modern life?
item.description: To truly revitalise a language, it must belong to the messy, everyday realities of its speakers.
item.content:encoded:
For over two decades, an extraordinary cultural and political experiment has unfolded along the mist-shrouded slopes of the Himalayas. The state government of Uttarakhand set out to construct a network of saṃskṛta-grāms – dedicated “Sanskrit-speaking” villages designed to transform the region into a living, breathing Sanskrit wonderland. Crores of rupees were poured into local administrations with a bold vision: resurrecting the “Language of the Gods” from its classical and liturgical repose and embedding it into the soil of everyday rural Indian life.

Yet, year after year, this ambitious policy narrative undergoes a curious ritual of its own.It is repeatedly re-released, temporarily mobilising ideological enthusiasts, only to stall amid bureaucratic quietude and persistent allegations of corruption. Initially promised for every administrative block and district, the actual mapping of operational Sanskrit villages has been drastically reduced to a sparse handful of locations.

item.title: Is calisthenics an effective form of exercise or just another fitness fad?
item.description: Learning to move your own body, control it and gradually make it stronger is one of the simplest, cheapest ways to start training.
item.content:encoded:
Calisthenics has gained enormous popularity in recent years, particularly thanks to social media and the rise of workout areas in city parks. You probably know some of the moves already, like pull-ups, push-ups, dips and squats.

For the more advanced, it also includes eye-catching, gravity-defying moves like the muscle-up, planche (where the body is held horizontal, supported solely by the hands) or the front lever (where the body is held horizontally while hanging from a bar).

But is calisthenics an effective form of exercise, or just another fitness fad? To answer this question, we first need to clarify what it is.

Calisthenics is a form of training that mainly uses a person’s own body weight as resistance. Its name derives from the Greek terms kállos (“beautiful”) and sthenos (“strength”), though the word’s modern use only caught on during the 19th century, when it referred to various forms of physical exercise.

Today, it includes well-known exercises such as squats, lunges, push-ups, pull-ups and dips, but calisthenics is not inherently acrobatic. Anyone who starts by doing a simple wall push-up is using the same principle as someone doing a one-arm push-up on the ground: moving their body against gravity.

item.title: Literary tourism: Why the places we love in books can never quite be found in real life
item.description: Literary geography, which combines physical geography with literary studies, emerged as the novel became popular and grew alongside literary tourism.
item.content:encoded:
From the Brontës’ Haworth to Jane Austen’s Bath, Wordsworth’s Lake District and Thomas Hardy’s Dorset, literary places continue to exert a powerful hold over readers.

Literary tourism appears to be enjoying renewed popularity, from visits inspired by classic novels to the TikTok trend of turning books into travel itineraries. But what exactly are literary tourists hoping to find when they get there? The answer is more complicated than it might seem.

Haworth, Bath and Dorset all exist, obviously. They can be found on a map and visited. But the Brontë moors, Austen’s Bath, Wordsworth’s Lakes and Hardy’s Wessex are also literary reimaginings of those places. They may never have existed in quite the form readers imagine.

Our fascination with literary places has a long history. Literary geography, which combines physical geography with literary studies, emerged in the late 19th century as the novel grew in popularity and, in many ways, grew alongside literary tourism.

In 1899, William Lyon Phelps created his Literary Map of England, marking locations associated with authors and literary works. A few years later, William Sharp’s Literary Geography (1904) mapped regions such as “Dickens land”, “the Brontë country” and the literary geography of the English lakes.

These early literary maps invited readers to see where fictional and geographical worlds appeared to overlap. More than...

item.title: Google Earth’s disastrous AI image generation experiment shows need for guardrails
item.description: In 24 hours, the feature introduced on July 30 was deployed to distort satellite imagery amid the US and Israel conflict with Iran.
item.content:encoded:
This article was originally published in Rest of World, which covers technology’s impact outside the West.

Since Israel and the US launched strikes against Iran in February, plunging the Gulf region into conflict, the countries have also been waging an information war using tools powered by artificial intelligence. To separate fact from fiction, authorities, analysts, and journalists alike turned to commercial satellite imagery, including Google Earth, the closest thing to “ground truth,” with limited access to sites.

Google Earth has long been a trusted infrastructure for the verification field, and is the platform on which open-source investigators are formally trained for conflict work in Syria, Yemen, and Sudan. Yet on July 30, Google launched a new feature that built image generation directly into Google Earth, the product that for two decades was synonymous with satellite image truth.

China’s used car dealers have set an expiry date for electric cars.

About four out of five used car dealers in China refuse to accept a fully electric vehicle older than five years, over worries about battery life and replacement costs, according to the International Energy Agency’s Global EV Outlook. A three-year-old EV in China now resells for about 45% of its original price, down from almost 55% in 2023, according to the China Automobile Dealers Association.

China has been the world’s largest EV market for a decade and now has 44 million of them on its roads. This makes it the first country where EVs are aging in large numbers. item.title: The bid to improve safety in public parks cannot involve keeping the public out
item.description: Rather than rushing in with stopgap fixes, the authorities must nurture a sense of ownership and respond to the concerns and needs of communities.
item.content:encoded:
On Monday, a 17-year-old was allegedly gang raped in a public park in Delhi by three men claiming to be from the police. Her 17-year-old male friend was beaten. The three men are reported to have told the friends that they faced potential legal trouble, separated them and then sexually assaulted the girl.

As the attack sparked concerns about safety in public parks in the national capital, the Delhi Development Authority said it would restrict entry to these spaces after sunset, install security cameras at the gates and increase surveillance by the police and security guards.

item.description: Devi had once said that ‘a responsible writer, standing at a turning point in history, has to take a stand in defence of the exploited.’

Picture a classroom in rural India. The textbook chapter on the freedom struggle lists your regular names – Gandhi, Nehru, Bose, Patel – with familiar photographs. In such a setting, it’s natural that a young tribal girl once asked Mahasweta Devi, “When we go to school, we read about Mahatma Gandhi. Did we have no heroes? Did we always suffer like this?”

The question assumes its own answer. If your stories aren’t told, your gods are not worshipped in temples, your warriors are not commemorated in statues, then perhaps – or so the logic goes – you had no stories, no gods, no warriors.

Just like how they inspire millions, stories can also disempower millions. India has always had a strange relationship with its stories and mythologies. Our mythologies afflict the afflicted, uplift the uplifted. They maintain the status quo, console the powerful, and justify caste and gender hierarchies.

item.title: Instead of pushing hard at exercise, try ‘slow jogging’
item.description: Exercise does not have to be intense to improve health.
item.content:encoded:
Avid runners are often chasing speed. Whether that’s improving their 5K or shaving seconds off their marathon time to nail a personal best. The idea that exercise should involve pushing further, harder or faster has long been embedded in fitness culture.

But against this backdrop, some people have adopted the almost counter-cultural belief that the key to fitness is to take things slow.

The growing popularity of the “slow jogging” trend online counters a lot of what we’ve been taught about fitness. Rather than striving for speed, the slow jogging trend encourages people to take short steps and move at a pace slow enough to comfortably hold a conversation.

To some people, this might look too easy to count as exercise. But exercise does not have to be intense to improve health.

The slow jogging trend was originally developed by a Japanese researcher named Hiroaki Tanaka. According to the researcher, jogging at “niko-niko pace” which translates to “smiling pace”) could be a more enjoyable way to improve cardiovascular fitness. The trend eventually caught on in South Korea before going viral online, where it is now being adopted by people all around the world.

He was the khalifa or steward of the Dilli Gharana, a strictly patriarchal lineage of hereditary Muslim musicians entrenched in the chaos of the old city. item.title: ‘The leaves tremble to your tune’: These poems ask enduring questions about mortality and meaning
item.description: An excerpt from ‘The Two Pits: New and Selected Poems’, by Siddhartha Menon.
item.content:encoded:
Playtime

And what do we foretell
of the kids beneath these high windows?
Through all the goings on a stab
right out of Bruegel’s Children’s Games:
“Can I play with you?” and feet
after a painted tyre
faltering: “Let me also play…?”
The world has come to a standstill.
The evening birds that oversee the play-space
are silenced. Like psephologists
at the time of a big verdict
we glance obliquely at a cluttered scene
and smile uncertainty aside.


Fat Cat

This cat is low-slung
with a belly full of bombs.
It was beneath the car
and has made it to the undergrowth
where all you see is a tail twitching
as if it were a tiger.
But this is no make believe:
its payload is real
and deadly. A matter of moments
in wariness
for populations to explode.


To A Rich Young Girl

It feels so good to her
the tug on her waist-length hair
being brushed as she stands in the garden
her eyes shut to the early
filter of sun as her head
is gently rocked with each
downward stroke it feels
so good
and with translucence
warming her eyelids and birdsong
turning on the sky
the universe is hers
to toy with where she stands.


The Pencil

Prospectives prowl the corridor
to sniff out whether one day that towel askew
could be their child’s.

They are meeting here for the first time
like tourists on a conducted tour
in a coach with meshed windows.

Their voices merge then separate
tinged with nervous wonder...

There are better ways to spend the early hours of a Friday morning than waiting in Dhaka for a prime minister to speak in New York. Journalism, unfortunately, does not always offer them.

I was on the graveyard shift, waiting for Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s maiden address to the United Nations General Assembly. My calculation put him at the lectern at around 4.30 am Dhaka time. So I did what journalists do while waiting for history to happen: I scrolled through the programme and listened to other people making history instead.

Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley was speaking – eloquent and considerably more effective than the average United Nations address, a genre in which 15 minutes can occasionally feel like a geological era.

Then I noticed a familiar name farther down the speakers’ list: Balendra “Balen” Shah, the 36-year-old prime minister of Nepal. That was enough to keep me awake.

Nepal is one of my favourite countries and, as an avid trekker, one I have visited repeatedly. But there was another, admittedly less statesmanlike, reason for staying up. I wanted to know whether the rapper-turned-mayor-turned-prime-minister would actually address the United Nations wearing his trademark black sunglasses.

In April, the energy crisis triggered by the conflict in West Asia ate into the meagre incomes of working-class Indians, precipitating a cost-of-living crisis for many of them. Thousands of workers hit the streets in Noida, an industrial city in the National Capital Region, to demand an increase in their minimum wage, which had not been revised since 2014.

The government of Uttar Pradesh responded by detaining hundreds of protesters, some of whom have spent months in jail.

This is the story of three such women – a factory worker who doubled up as an activist, a domestic worker who was inspired by the workers to demand better working conditions for herself, and an artist who joined the protests in solidarity.

Two out of these three women remain behind bars because the police have filed nearly a dozen cases against them for allegedly inciting violence during the agitation. Scroll made several visits to Noida to piece together this account of their lives.

item.content:encoded:
Bharatiya Janata Party MLAs in Jammu and Kashmir on Friday protested against a reference to a 2000 autonomy resolution made in a fresh one moved by Chief Minister Omar Abdullah seeking statehood for the Union Territory, The Telegraph reported.

The text of the fresh resolution moved by Abdullah on Friday says that in addition to the resolutions passed by the Assembly in June 2000 and November 2024, the House was calling on the Union government to urgently restore Jammu and Kashmir’s statehood.

In June 2000, the National Conference government led by Farooq Abdullah passed a resolution in the Assembly calling for restoration of greater autonomy to Jammu and Kashmir as it existed before August 1953. However, it was rejected by the then-Atal Bihari Vajpayee government at the Centre.

In November 2024, the Assembly passed another resolution calling for the restoration of the special status the erstwhile state had under Article 370 of the Constitution, which was abrogated by the Union government in August 2019.

During the Assembly proceedings on Friday, BJP MLAs entered the well of the House and tore copies of the resolution following the reference to the 2000 resolution, The Telegraph reported.

The speaker adjourned the proceedings for the day after a scuffle between legislators.

In its note while returning the draft legislation, the Union government said that the the bill’s definition of “goonda”, which includes a person who commits, attempts to commit, abets, promotes, finances or facilitates offences punishable under the 1985 Act, may overlap with the preventive detention framework provided under the central 1988 Prevention of Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act.

The proposed legislation may create a parallel preventive-detention mechanism in cases of drug-related activities and may lead to inconsistencies between the laws at the state and the central levels, the Union government said.

It recommended that the reference to offences under the 1985 Act be deleted from the bill to avoid duplication.
